name: Vansen Pressline Work Henley
description:
A heavy-duty three-button henley made for people who work with their hands. The fabric is Vansen's signature GritWeave — a dense synth-cotton composite that resists minor abrasions and holds up to repeated industrial washing without pilling or fading. Raglan sleeves allow full arm mobility, and the reinforced shoulder panels are triple-stitched. Comes in two colors: off-white and a dark charcoal called 'Forge.' The chest pocket is sized to hold a data chip or a folded work order.

Vansen makes workwear the way workwear should be made — without frills. The Pressline Henley is issued to workers at several Tier 2 manufacturing floors as optional uniform-adjacent clothing, which means you see it everywhere from assembly lines to freight yards to the weekend market.
what_it_says: You work for a living and you're not embarrassed about it. You buy clothes that last, not clothes that impress.
story_hooks: The charcoal colorway has become an informal identifier for members of a Tier 2 labor organizing cell — wearing it to a meeting means you're sympathetic.
A character wears one as a disguise to blend into a factory floor they have no business being on.
Someone finds a work order folded in the chest pocket of a secondhand one — the job listed was never completed.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian henley with a sturdy, no-nonsense silhouette. The raglan sleeves create a relaxed shoulder line that reads as functional rather than fashionable. The three-button placket sits centered on the chest, with a single patch pocket below. Overall impression is blue-collar dependable—the kind of garment that disappears into the background of a working person's day.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the torso with enough room for layering or movement without being oversized. The raglan cut allows full arm mobility without binding. Sits naturally at the hips, slightly longer than a t-shirt but not long enough to tuck. Designed for comfort during sustained physical work.
physical_description.primary_material: GritWeave — a dense synth-cotton composite engineered by Vansen for durability and abuse resistance. Not fully synthetic, not fully natural; a practical hybrid that resists pilling, minor abrasions, and industrial washing cycles.
physical_description.texture: Slightly textured surface with a subtle nap from the composite weave. Feels substantial in hand—heavier than casual cotton but not stiff. The fabric has a matte finish that hides minor dirt and wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Two utilitarian options: off-white (industrial neutral, shows wear) and 'Forge' charcoal (dark gray-black, hides grime). Both are desaturated, practical colorways with no branding or pattern.
physical_description.closures: Three buttons down the placket, likely coated polymer or industrial-grade metal. Functional rather than decorative. No collar closure—it's a loose henley neckline.
distinctive_features: Triple-stitched reinforced shoulder panels for durability under repetitive strain
Raglan sleeves for unrestricted arm movement
Chest pocket sized specifically for data chips or folded work orders
GritWeave composite fabric resistant to pilling and abrasion
Designed to withstand repeated industrial washing without fading
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2–3 functional wear. Issued as optional uniform at corporate manufacturing floors, but affordable and ubiquitous enough to cross into Tier 3 streetwear. Signals working-class labor without poverty.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by assembly line workers, freight handlers, maintenance staff, and anyone whose job involves physical durability. Also common at weekend markets and casual social spaces in working districts. Wearing this signals competence, practicality, and an absence of pretension. It's the uniform of the GLMZ working body.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in rather than pristine. After a few washes and weeks of wear, it softens slightly but maintains shape. Minor fraying at seams is normal. Stains from work (grease, dust, marking pen) are expected and don't ruin the garment. A well-worn Pressline Henley shows its durability by looking better with age, not worse.

image_prompt: A worn Vansen Pressline Work Henley in charcoal 'Forge' displayed on a broad-shouldered mannequin or draped over a muscular neo-noir model with visible subcutaneous tech scars. The garment shows subtle signs of industrial use—faint grease marks, threadbare patches at the shoulders from repetitive work. Moody warehouse lighting from above, casting deep shadows across the reinforced seams and triple-stitched shoulder panels. The chest pocket is visible and detailed.
